prompt: Which comparison of single-mode and multimode fiber is accurate?
options: Multimode supports longer links because it has a larger core.
Either fiber type is interchangeable when the connector is LC.
Single-mode has a smaller core and is common on longer links.
Jacket color alone proves the installed fiber's speed and reach.
explanation: Single-mode fiber has the smaller core and is the usual choice for long links. Actual reach depends on the module and fiber pairing.

whyWrong.0: A larger core does not extend reach; multimode light paths limit distance.
whyWrong.1: A matching connector does not make the fiber type and optics compatible.
whyWrong.3: Jacket color does not establish a fiber’s speed or reach; use the verified specification.

prompt: An office plans 90 m of installed cable plus 10 m of patch leads for 10GBASE-T switch ports. Which category supports the full 100 m channel?
options: Cat6A
Cat6 for an unspecified installation
Cat5 rated for 100BASE-TX
Cat5e rated for 1000BASE-T
explanation: Cat6A supports 10GBASE-T over a full 100 m channel. The permanent link and patch leads together count toward the 100 m.

whyWrong.1: Cat6 carries 10GBASE-T only to about 55 m.
whyWrong.2: Cat5 rated for 100BASE-TX is not a 10GBASE-T cable.
whyWrong.3: Cat5e is the normal 1 Gbps choice and does not carry 10GBASE-T.

prompt: A conventional 10/100 Ethernet crossover exchanges the transmit and receive pairs. Which pin mapping describes that exchange?
options: Pins 1↔2 and 3↔6, without moving pairs
Pins 1↔3 and 2↔6 between the ends
Pins 1↔1 through 8↔8 between the ends
explanation: A conventional 10/100 crossover swaps pins 1 and 2 with pins 3 and 6, so each end’s transmit pair meets the other end’s receive pair.

whyWrong.0: Reversing all eight pins describes a rollover cable.
whyWrong.1: Swapping conductors within a pair is not a transmit/receive crossover.
whyWrong.3: The same pin at both ends describes a straight-through cable.

prompt: Which Cisco switch command provides a compact table of port status, VLAN, duplex, speed and media type?
options: show ip route
show running-config
show power inline
show interfaces status
explanation: `show interfaces status` gives one line per port with status, VLAN, duplex, speed and media type. Use `show interfaces <port>` for one port’s counters and state.

whyWrong.0: The routing table has no switch-port status columns.
whyWrong.1: The running configuration shows configured commands, not operational state.
whyWrong.2: `show power inline` shows PoE allocation, not Ethernet port state.

prompt: What does a late collision on a half-duplex 10/100 Ethernet link mean?
options: A frame waited in the output queue beyond its allowed time.
A receive frame failed the Ethernet FCS check.
The peer advertised an unsupported link speed during negotiation.
A collision occurred beyond the permitted collision window.
explanation: A late collision is a collision detected after the allowed collision window. Check duplex agreement and the physical path.

whyWrong.0: Output queuing is a different mechanism from collision timing.
whyWrong.1: A failed FCS check is received-frame corruption, counted as a CRC error.
whyWrong.2: Autonegotiation capabilities do not define the late-collision counter.

prompt: Assume traditional 10/100 MDI/MDI-X ports with no auto-MDIX. Which two connections require a crossover cable? (Choose two.)
options: PC to switch
Switch to switch
Router Ethernet port to switch
PC to router Ethernet port
Server Ethernet port to switch
explanation: Like devices (switch to switch, PC to router) use the same MDI arrangement and need a crossover. Unlike devices (PC, server or router to switch) use straight-through.

whyWrong.0: A PC pairs MDI with the switch’s MDI-X, so straight-through is correct.
whyWrong.2: A router Ethernet port pairs MDI with the switch’s MDI-X.
whyWrong.4: A server pairs MDI with the switch’s MDI-X, so straight-through is correct.

spec.title: One switch and a shared hub segment
spec.caption: PC-C and PC-D share the hub segment; all switch ports belong to VLAN 1.

prompt: All switch ports are in VLAN 1, and there are no routers or additional links. How many Ethernet collision domains and broadcast domains are represented?
options: One collision domain and three broadcast domains
Four collision domains and one broadcast domain
Three collision domains and three broadcast domains
Three collision domains and one broadcast domain
explanation: Each connected switch port is its own collision domain, so there are three. The two PCs on HUB1 share one of them, and all ports are in one VLAN, so there is one broadcast domain.

whyWrong.0: One VLAN is one broadcast domain, whatever the number of segments.
whyWrong.1: The two PCs on the hub share one collision domain, which gives three, not four.
whyWrong.2: Ports in the same VLAN do not make separate broadcast domains.

prompt: A 350 m path will use 10GBASE-SR modules. The supported reaches are 300 m on OM3 and 400 m on OM4. Which choice meets the stated distance?
options: OM4 multimode fiber within the specified SR design
OM3 multimode fiber because both ends use SR
Single-mode fiber because its core is smaller
Cat6A copper because the connectors can be adapted
explanation: 350 m exceeds the 300 m OM3 reach but is within the 400 m OM4 reach. OM4 multimode meets the distance.

whyWrong.1: Matching SR modules do not extend OM3 beyond 300 m.
whyWrong.2: SR is specified here for multimode fiber, not single-mode.
whyWrong.3: SR is optical, and 350 m exceeds the 100 m copper channel limit.

prompt: A duplex fiber patch connects Switch A Tx to Switch B Tx and Switch A Rx to Switch B Rx. Both modules are otherwise compatible. What should be corrected first?
options: Connect each transmitter to the far receiver.
Leave the mapping and replace one module with a different optical standard.
Leave the mapping and clean both connectors before any other change.
Loop each transmitter to its own receiver instead of the far device.
explanation: On a duplex optical link each transmitter must connect to the far end’s receiver. Tx-to-Tx is a polarity fault, so swap the strands.

whyWrong.1: The modules are already compatible, so changing the standard does not fix the strand mapping.
whyWrong.2: Cleaning does not correct a Tx-to-Tx connection.
whyWrong.3: A local loopback gives no communication between the two switches.

exhibit.title: Supplied optical measurements — teaching example
exhibit.text:
Receive power: -16.0 dBm
Acceptable range for this exercise: -12.0 to -1.0 dBm
Link state: down

prompt: The optical receiver’s acceptable range is −12 through −1 dBm. What does a receive reading of −16 dBm show?
options: The signal exceeds the receiver's upper power limit.
The receive power is below the supplied lower limit.
The fiber polarity is definitely the only fault.
Both transmit modules are confirmed healthy.
explanation: −16 dBm is below the −12 dBm lower limit, so the receiver gets too little light. The reading alone does not say whether the cause is the fiber, connectors or the far transmitter.

whyWrong.0: A reading above −1 dBm would exceed the upper limit.
whyWrong.2: Polarity, distance, connectors, mismatched modules or a weak transmitter can all cause low power.
whyWrong.3: One receive reading does not show that both transmitters are healthy.

exhibit.title: Two ends of one physical cable — representative state
exhibit.text:
SW1 FastEthernet0/24: administratively down, protocol down
SW2 FastEthernet0/24: down, protocol down
SW1 interface configuration: shutdown
SW2 interface configuration: no shutdown

prompt: The cable directly connects the two listed ports. The intended design enables both. What does the evidence establish?
options: Both switches are administratively shut down because both links are down.
SW2 must have a cable defect because its port is administratively enabled.
SW2 should also be shut down to match SW1 before testing traffic.
SW1 is administratively disabled; SW2’s down state does not identify a separate fault.
explanation: SW1 is administratively shut down, which explains the local down state. SW2 loses link because its peer is disabled, although SW2 itself is enabled.

whyWrong.0: Only SW1 has the shutdown command.
whyWrong.1: A down far end is what SW1’s shutdown produces; it does not show a cable defect.
whyWrong.2: The design enables both ports, and shutting down SW2 would not restore the link.

exhibit.title: Representative: SW1# show interfaces status
exhibit.text:
Port      Name          Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Fa0/3     Appliance     connected    1          a-half  a-100 10/100BaseTX

prompt: The appliance is manually set to 100 Mbps full duplex. Its connected switch port is automatic and shows the following state. What has been established?
options: The link reports a matching speed but an undetermined duplex.
The two ends report matching speed but opposing duplex.
The a- prefix means the switch follows the forced full-duplex setting.
The connected state establishes matching speed and duplex.
explanation: The appliance is full duplex while the switch shows a-half, so the operational duplex settings disagree. On 10/100, an auto end detects a forced end’s speed but not its duplex, so it falls back to half.

whyWrong.0: The switch explicitly reports half duplex.
whyWrong.2: The a- prefix means the setting was negotiated automatically, and here the result is half duplex.
whyWrong.3: A link can show connected even with a duplex mismatch.

prompt: On the half-duplex end of a 10/100 duplex mismatch, which two observations are consistent with its collision-handling behavior? (Choose two.)
options: The collision count increases during simultaneous traffic.
The late-collision count increases during the test.
The CRC count identifies the exact damaged cable segment.
The output-drop count measures collisions at the far receiver.
The collision count must fall when the duplex setting is repaired.
explanation: The half-duplex end uses collision detection while the full-duplex peer transmits freely. Collisions and late collisions therefore increase under simultaneous traffic.

whyWrong.2: CRC errors count corrupted received frames and do not locate a cable segment.
whyWrong.3: Output drops relate to egress queuing, not collisions at the far end.
whyWrong.4: Fixing the duplex stops new collisions, but existing counter totals do not fall.

prompt: A 10/100 link has a forced 100/full endpoint and an automatic switch port operating at 100/half. Both support autonegotiation. What is the preferred starting repair?
options: Leave the current settings and inspect only the next IP hop.
Return both ends to auto and verify speed, duplex and traffic.
Return only the forced end’s speed to auto but leave its duplex forced.
Clear the counters on both ends without changing their settings.
explanation: Setting both ends to auto lets them negotiate matching speed and duplex. Setting both manually to matching values also works.

whyWrong.0: The duplex disagreement is on the link and needs correcting.
whyWrong.2: Fixing only the speed leaves the duplex forced, so the mismatch can remain.
whyWrong.3: Clearing counters does not change the settings.

exhibit.title: Printer port before and after an authorized correction
exhibit.text:
Before: administratively down, protocol down
Change applied: no shutdown
After: up, protocol up
Printer address and mask: match the documented plan

prompt: The printer was unreachable before its port was enabled. Which verification best establishes that the required service is restored?
options: Read the interface again and stop because up/up establishes printing.
Save the configuration immediately because no shutdown was accepted.
Retest reachability and a new print request, then record the result.
Clear all interface counters so the display begins with zero errors.
explanation: Link up/up shows the port works, but the goal is a working printer. Retest reachability and a real print request, then save the verified configuration.

whyWrong.0: Link state is necessary evidence but does not test the printing service.
whyWrong.1: An accepted command and a save do not show the service is available.
whyWrong.3: Clearing counters neither tests nor repairs the service.

exhibit.title: Representative counter comparison — same interface
exhibit.text:
Start of test: 4 input errors, 4 CRC
End of test:   89 input errors, 89 CRC
Both ends: 1000 Mbps, full duplex

prompt: Both ends of a copper link show 1 Gbps full duplex. During a controlled transfer, received CRC errors increase on the switch. What is the best next action?
options: Clear the counters and conclude the physical path is repaired.
Replace the cable immediately without collecting another reading.
Test the cable path and compare the far-end error readings.
Treat matching duplex as proof that these errors are harmless.
explanation: Rising CRC errors mean received frames are failing the error check even though speed and duplex match. Test the cable path and compare the far end’s error counters.

whyWrong.0: Clearing a counter removes evidence and repairs nothing.
whyWrong.1: A cable fault is likely, but the counter alone does not prove which component is bad.
whyWrong.3: Matching duplex does not make corrupted frames acceptable.

prompt: How many wire pairs does 1000BASE-T use?
options: One pair
Two pairs
Three pairs
Four pairs
explanation: 1000BASE-T uses all four pairs. 100BASE-TX uses only two.

whyWrong.0: No twisted-pair Ethernet standard in this chapter uses a single pair.
whyWrong.2: No standard here uses three pairs.

prompt: Roughly how far does Cat6 carry 10GBASE-T?
options: About 55 m
About 100 m
About 150 m
About 300 m
explanation: Cat6 carries 10GBASE-T only to about 55 m. Cat6A is needed for a full 100 m channel.

whyWrong.1: 100 m is the 10GBASE-T channel length on Cat6A.
whyWrong.2: 150 m exceeds the twisted-pair channel limit.
whyWrong.3: 300 m is an OM3 fiber reach, not copper.

prompt: What is the normal collision behavior on a full-duplex Ethernet link?
options: No collisions occur
Collisions occur only on 1 Gbps links
Collisions occur whenever both ends send
Collisions occur once per frame
explanation: On a full-duplex link, normal operation has no collisions, because each direction has its own path.

whyWrong.1: Link speed does not cause collisions on a full-duplex link.
whyWrong.2: Full duplex lets both ends send at once without colliding.
whyWrong.3: Collisions are not part of normal frame transmission.

prompt: What is the normal minimum copper category for new 1 Gbps cabling?
options: Cat5
Cat5e
Cat3
Cat6A
explanation: Cat5e is the normal minimum choice for new 1 Gbps cabling.

whyWrong.2: Cat3 is far below what Gigabit Ethernet needs.
whyWrong.3: Cat6A works but is not the minimum; it is needed for full-distance 10GBASE-T.
